title: The canonical maps of formal glueing: localized S-module structure, swap of two localizations, localization of a base change
statement:
Let $\varphi:R\to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings, let $P$ be an $R$-module and $f,g\in R$. For an $R$-module $Q$ and $e\in R$ let $Q_e$ be the localization of $Q$ at $e$ with its localization map $Q\to Q_e$, $q\mapsto q/1$ [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away], and for an $R$-linear map $h:Q\to Q'$ let $h_e:Q_e\to Q'_e$, $q/e^n\mapsto h(q)/e^n$, be its localization [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]; $Q\otimes_RS$ and $h\otimes_RS$ are the base changes [def-weil-module-base-change], and an $S$-module is regarded as an $R$-module through $\varphi$.
(1) For $R$-linear maps $k:Q\to Q'$, $h:Q'\to Q''$ and $h':Q'\to Q''$ one has $(h\circ k)_e=h_e\circ k_e$, $(h+h')_e=h_e+h'_e$ and $(\mathrm{id}_Q)_e=\mathrm{id}_{Q_e}$. Consequently, if $Q$ is an $S$-module, the maps $(s\cdot)_e:Q_e\to Q_e$, $s\in S$ (the localizations of the multiplications $q\mapsto sq$), make $Q_e$ an $S$-module, i.e. $s\cdot(q/e^n)=(sq)/e^n$, whose underlying $R$-module structure is the given one; the localization map $Q\to Q_e$ is $S$-linear; and $h_e$ is $S$-linear whenever $h:Q\to Q'$ is an $S$-linear map of $S$-modules.
(2) The elements $f$ and $g$ act bijectively on the $R$-module $(P_g)_f$, and there is exactly one $R$-linear map $\sigma^P_{f,g}:(P_f)_g\to(P_g)_f$ with $\sigma^P_{f,g}((p/1)/1)=(p/1)/1$ for all $p\in P$. It is given by $\sigma^P_{f,g}((p/f^a)/g^b)=(p/g^b)/f^a$ ($p\in P$, $a,b\ge0$), and it is an isomorphism with inverse $\sigma^P_{g,f}$.
(3) The element $f$ acts bijectively on $P_f\otimes_RS$, and there is exactly one $R$-linear map $c^P_f:(P\otimes_RS)_f\to P_f\otimes_RS$ with $c^P_f((p\otimes s)/1)=(p/1)\otimes s$ for all $p\in P$, $s\in S$. It is given by $c^P_f((p\otimes s)/f^e)=(p/f^e)\otimes s$, it is $S$-linear for the $S$-module structure of (1) on $(P\otimes_RS)_f$, and it is an isomorphism of $S$-modules.

source.place: More on Algebra, Remark 05EL (label remark-glueing-data, line 24641): the 'canonical isomorphisms' can_i : (M ⊗_R S)_{f_i} → M_{f_i} ⊗_R S and can_ij : (M_{f_i})_{f_j} → (M_{f_j})_{f_i} of the functor Can, used implicitly in conditions (a), (b) of the objects; existence and uniqueness from Algebra Lemma 07K0 (algebra.tex line 1171, label lemma-universal-property-localization-module); (P ⊗_R S)_f ≅ P_f ⊗_R S from Algebra Lemma 00DK (line 2088, label lemma-tensor-localization)

proof.text: For $R$-linear $k:Q\to Q'$ and $h:Q'\to Q''$, the maps $(h\circ k)_e$ and $h_e\circ k_e$ both send $q/e^n$ to $h(k(q))/e^n$; likewise $(h+h')_e$ and $h_e+h'_e$ send it to $(h(q)+h'(q))/e^n$, and $(\mathrm{id}_Q)_e(q/e^n)=q/e^n$. Every element of $Q_e$ is such a fraction, so the three maps in (1) are equal.

source.place: Algebra, Definition 07JZ (definition-localization-module) and the fraction construction preceding it, for the powers of e

proof.text: For an $S$-module $Q$, multiplication $m_s:q\mapsto sq$ is $R$-linear since the images of $R$ commute with $s$. The identities $m_1=\mathrm{id}$, $m_{s+t}=m_s+m_t$ and $m_{st}=m_s\circ m_t$ remain true after localization by the preceding step. They therefore define an $S$-module structure on $Q_e$, with $s(q/e^n)=(sq)/e^n$. If $s=\varphi(r)$, this is the original $R$-action on fractions, so its restricted $R$-module structure is unchanged; $q\mapsto q/1$ is $S$-linear by the same formula. For an $S$-linear $h:Q\to Q'$, $h_e(s(q/e^n))=h(sq)/e^n=s(h(q)/e^n)$, proving the last assertion of (1).

source.place: More on Algebra, Remark 05EL (remark-glueing-data), S-module localizations used for can_i and morphisms; fraction construction in Algebra, Definition 07JZ

proof.text: The element $f$ acts bijectively on $(P_g)_f$ by its outer localization. Multiplication by $g$ is already invertible on $P_g$, and localizing its inverse as an $R$-linear map gives an inverse to multiplication by $g$ on $(P_g)_f$, by the composition and identity formulas of step 1. Hence both $f$ and $g$ act bijectively on $(P_g)_f$.

source.place: Algebra, Definition 07JZ (definition-localization-module) and Lemma 07K0 (lemma-universal-property-localization-module), specialized to powers of f and g

proof.text: Compose $P\to P_g\to(P_g)_f$. Since $f$ acts bijectively on its target, Lemma 07K0's universal property gives a unique $R$-linear map $u:P_f\to(P_g)_f$ taking $p/1$ to $(p/1)/1$; its fraction formula is $u(p/f^a)=(p/1)/f^a$. Since $g$ also acts bijectively on the target, the same property extends $u$ uniquely to $\sigma^P_{f,g}:(P_f)_g\to(P_g)_f$, with $\sigma^P_{f,g}((p/f^a)/g^b)=(p/g^b)/f^a$. Any other map with the stated values on $((p/1)/1)$ first agrees with $u$ on $P_f$, then agrees with this extension on $(P_f)_g$, so the asserted uniqueness holds.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 07K0 (lemma-universal-property-localization-module), applied twice; More on Algebra, Remark 05EL (remark-glueing-data), canonical can_ij

proof.text: Interchanging $f$ and $g$ in step 4 constructs $\sigma^P_{g,f}$. Their two composites send each $((p/f^a)/g^b)$ and $((p/g^b)/f^a)$ back to itself by the displayed fraction formula. Such fractions exhaust the respective iterated localizations, so the maps are inverse isomorphisms, proving (2). This also covers $f=0$, $g=0$, or a zero localization: the same universal property and formulas apply.

source.place: More on Algebra, Remark 05EL (remark-glueing-data), canonical isomorphisms can_ij; fraction construction in Algebra, Definition 07JZ

proof.text: Tensor the localization map $P\to P_f$ with $S$ to obtain the $R$-linear map $t:P\otimes_RS\to P_f\otimes_RS$, $p\otimes s\mapsto(p/1)\otimes s$. Multiplication by $f$ is invertible on $P_f$ and hence on its tensor product with $S$ (its inverse tensored with the identity is inverse there). Lemma 07K0 therefore extends $t$ uniquely to an $R$-linear map $c^P_f:(P\otimes_RS)_f\to P_f\otimes_RS$. The extension formula gives $c^P_f((p\otimes s)/f^e)=(p/f^e)\otimes s$. Pure tensors generate $P\otimes_RS$, and every localized element has a fraction representative, so this formula determines the extension and its values on $(p\otimes s)/1$ prove the uniqueness asserted in (3). By the $S$-module structure in step 2, both $c^P_f(s'((p\otimes s)/f^e))$ and $s'c^P_f((p\otimes s)/f^e)$ equal $(p/f^e)\otimes s's$; additivity and generation by localized pure tensors prove $S$-linearity.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 07K0 (lemma-universal-property-localization-module) and Lemma 00DK (lemma-tensor-localization); More on Algebra, Remark 05EL (remark-glueing-data), canonical can_i

proof.text: The localization-after-tensor theorem [lem-weil-pbc-localization-tensor-over-base], applied with $A=R$, $M=P$, $T=\{1,f,f^2,\dots\}$ and $N=S$, says that $t$ is a localization at the powers of $f$ and that its induced $R$-linear map $(P\otimes_RS)_f\to P_f\otimes_RS$ is an isomorphism with precisely the formula of step 6. By the uniqueness in step 6 this induced map is $c^P_f$. Since $c^P_f$ is $S$-linear, its inverse is $S$-linear as well: for $y=c^P_f(x)$, $(c^P_f)^{-1}(sy)=(c^P_f)^{-1}(c^P_f(sx))=sx$. Thus $c^P_f$ is an $S$-module isomorphism.
